scene.excerpt: The Baba Yaga went out into the courtyard and whistled--before her appeared a mortar with a pestle and a broom. The red horseman appeared--the sun rose. The Baba Yaga seated herself in the mortar, and drove out of the courtyard, shooting herself along with the pestle, sweeping away her traces with the broom. Vasilissa was left alone, so she examined the Baba Yaga's house, wondered at the abundance there was in everything, and remained lost in thought as to which work she ought to take to first. She looked up;

narrativeBlocks.title: The hut that walks
narrativeBlocks.body: Deep in the forest stands a hut on chicken legs — it turns and dances and squats to let visitors in only when they ask the right way. Around it, a fence of bones; on the posts, skulls whose eyes burn at night.

narrativeBlocks.title: The old woman in the mortar
narrativeBlocks.body: Baba Yaga herself flies in a mortar, driving with a pestle, sweeping her tracks away with a broom. She is old beyond measure, iron-nosed, and always hungry for news of the outside.

narrativeBlocks.title: Both monster and test
narrativeBlocks.body: The tales never decide her: she eats the unwary, but for the right visitor — the courteous, the patient, the well-advised — she gives impossible tasks and then the help to pass them. She is the forest's gatekeeper, not simply its villain.

narrativeBlocks.title: The riders at the door
narrativeBlocks.body: At her gate pass three riders — white for dawn, red for day, black for night — the day's passage personified. Even time itself rides in her service; this witch stands at the world's hinges.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why she's everywhere
narrativeBlocks.body: Baba Yaga is the Slavic tradition's indispensable figure: the dangerous border between the everyday world and the deep forest where everything is possible. Every quest in this pack passes her gate.
